paper_claims.claim: Existing robot manipulation continual learning benchmarks entangle the raw speed of learning new interactions with the ability to reuse previous knowledge, which this benchmark isolates by ending each sequence with a composition task that recombines preceding primitives.

World models naturally partition into a task-agnostic backbone (encoder + dynamics) that must be learned continually and task-specific heads (reward, value, policy) that are re-initialized for each new task.
DreamerV3 consistently outperforms TD-MPC2 on both BWT and FWT across all CL methods due to its generative reconstruction objective capturing broad scene detail.

Conventional continual learning methods trade forward transfer against backward transfer; fine-tuning forgets most, ER has highest FWT but unbounded buffer, EWC fails at reuse (negative FWT), and PackNet achieves near-zero forgetting but capacity shrinks.
Difficulty rises monotonically along the composition axis: BWT worsens from action (Dreamer: 5.94, TD-MPC2: 32.15) to perception (11.79 / 57.81) to full composition (30.12 / 68.68).

Under the frozen-encoder diagnostic, modular PWM reaches BWT 3.85 and FWT 36.18 against TD-MPC2's 34.97 and 38.11, nearly eliminating forgetting while matching fine-tuning speed; but without a frozen encoder, PWM is on par with TD-MPC2 due to encoder representation drift.

Task-conditioned routing in PWM succeeds on Reach, Grasp, and BinPnP but struggles on temporally composed tasks (PnPBlock, DrawerPnP, PnPBoxClose) where different primitives are needed at different stages.
